entries.position: predeterminer before another determiner (all the money); central determiner before a bare noun (all children)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (all students) and uncountable nouns (all information); a singular countable only when another determiner follows (all my life, all this trouble) or the noun names a span of time (all day, all summer). Never a bare singular countable: ✗ all book, ✗ all student.
entries.ofRule: Optional before another determiner — all (of) the students, all (of) my cousins. Required before a personal pronoun — all of them, all of us; ✗ all them. Impossible before a bare noun — all children, ✗ all of children.
entries.pattern: all [plural/uncountable noun] / all (of) [the/my/these + noun] / all of [them/us/you] / [plural subject] + auxiliary + all + verb (floated) / all [day/week/year]
entries.contrast: all covers three or more, or an undivided mass; both covers exactly two. Against every, the difference is grammatical rather than semantic: all takes a plural noun and a plural verb and sees the group as one body (all the students were notified), while every takes a singular noun and a singular verb and runs down the list (every student was notified). Against not all, watch the scope — All the seats weren't taken is ambiguous in speech and should be rewritten as Not all the seats were taken (some were empty) or None of the seats were taken (all were empty). As a determiner all precedes a noun; standing alone it is a pronoun (All is well, That's all).
variants: all day / all week / all year
entries.meaning: Sweeps in the entire set or the entire quantity, with nothing left out. The verb agrees with the noun all is quantifying, not with all itself — All the money is gone but All the coins are gone. Like both and each, all can float away from its subject and land next to the verb: All the guests have left → The guests have all left.
examples: All the students passed the exam.
She spent all her savings on the down payment.
All of them showed up an hour early.
All this trouble started with one missed email. — a singular countable, grammatical only because this follows
We waited all day for a callback from the insurance company.
All information on this form is confidential.
The guests have all gone home.
All children learn to read at their own pace.

entries.respell: awl-uhn-SING-gyuh-lur · and takes its weak form /ən/ or a syllabic /n̩/, giving [ˌɔl n̩ ˈsɪŋɡjəlɚ]; all keeps /ɔl/, or /ɑl/ for the many Americans who merge cot and caught; the main stress lands on singular, whose /j/ is often dropped in fast speech to give [ˈsɪŋɡəlɚ]
entries.position: predeterminer — it stands in front of the central determiner, exactly where
entries.register: archaic legal boilerplate. An American meets it in deeds, wills, probate inventories, admiralty writs, and old insurance policies, and essentially nowhere else; plain-language drafting guides delete it on sight
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns, almost always inside a legal doublet of their own — all and singular the goods and chattels, all and singular the lands and tenements. It takes an uncountable noun only in a few frozen formulas (all and singular the personal property). Never a bare singular countable: ✗ all and singular the house, ✗ all and singular house.
entries.pattern: all and singular the [plural noun] · all and singular the [noun] and [noun] (the doublet doubled again) · to have and to hold all and singular the [noun] · all and singular, the [noun] (with the comma, as older deeds set it)
entries.contrast: Singular here does not mean "one" or "unusual." It is the Latin singuli, "one by one," arriving through Law French, so the phrase means "the whole set, and every item in it taken separately" — which makes it all and each welded into one predeterminer. It is the courtroom ancestor of the two doublets already in this file: any and all, which does the same belt-and-suspenders work in modern contracts, and each and every, which does it in speech. Against all and sundry, which looks parallel but is a pronoun meaning "everybody" and takes no noun at all (the party was open to all and sundry), all and singular always has a noun phrase after it; see sundry.
variants: all and sundry (a pronoun — a different word)
entries.meaning: With of: Never — ✗ all and singular of the goods. The doublet sits directly on top of the, exactly as predeterminer all does; the of form a modern reader expects, all of the goods, is the rewrite rather than a variant. An archaic legal predeterminer meaning "the entire set, and each member of it individually." It exists to defeat two opposite readings at once — that a grant covers the collection but not the pieces, or the pieces but not the collection — which is the same anxiety that produces any and all. The verb agrees with the plural noun, not with singular: All and singular the parcels are conveyed. Modern American drafters write all and stop.
examples: The deed conveys all and singular the lands and tenements described in Schedule A. — a conveyance
I give and bequeath all and singular my goods and chattels to my sister. — a will
The executor filed an inventory of all and singular the personal property of the estate. — probate
The policy insures all and singular the vessels named in the endorsement. — marine insurance, where the phrase is oldest
To have and to hold all and singular the premises, with the appurtenances thereto belonging. — the habendum clause of an old deed
A modern contract says all the property described above and loses nothing. — the plain-language rewrite

entries.position: predeterminer before another determiner (both the twins, both my parents); central determiner before a bare plural (both hands)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns only, and only when the set has exactly two — both hands, both candidates. Never a singular countable (✗ both hand), never an uncountable (✗ both furniture, ✗ both information), and never a set of three or more (✗ both of the five finalists).
entries.ofRule: Optional before another determiner — both (of) the twins, both (of) these windows. Required before a personal pronoun in this order — both of them, both of us; ✗ both them, though the reversed order them both is perfectly good (I saw them both). Not used before a bare plural — both parents, ✗ both of parents.
entries.pattern: both [plural countable noun] / both (of) [the/my/these + plural noun] / both of [them/us/you] / [plural subject] + are/have + both + … (floated)
entries.contrast: both is the plural member of the dual set, and the three of them split the verb neatly: both takes the two together and a plural verb (Both plans work), either takes one of the two and a singular verb (Either plan works), neither takes zero of the two and a singular verb (Neither plan works). Against all, both is capped at two — for three or more, all is the only choice. The correlative conjunction both … and joins two items and is a different word class entirely. As a determiner both precedes a noun; standing alone it is a pronoun (Both are broken).
entries.meaning: Refers to the two members of a two-member set together, as a pair. The verb is always plural, even though the sense is "each of the two" — Both of my parents are retired. Both floats like all and each: Both of my parents are retired → My parents are both retired. It sits badly with a negative — Both of them didn't come is ambiguous and avoided; say Neither of them came for zero, or Only one of them came for one.
examples: Both windows in the front room leak.
Both of my parents grew up in Cleveland.
She broke both her wrists in the fall.
Both candidates dodged the question.
I've read both of them, and neither is any good.
My sisters are both teachers.

entries.position: central determiner; also floats to a position beside the verb, and postposes as an adverb (ten dollars each)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — each student, each page, each day. Never a plural countable (✗ each students), never an uncountable (✗ each water, ✗ each advice). To reach a plural noun, each must go through of: each of the students.
entries.ofRule: Required before any noun phrase that already has a determiner, and before every pronoun — each of the students, each of my cousins, each of them. ✗ each my cousins and ✗ each them are ungrammatical. Bare each + singular noun takes no of: ✗ each of student.
entries.pattern: each [singular countable noun] / each of [the/my/these + plural noun] / each of [them/us/you] / [plural subject] + each + [plural verb] (floated) / [noun] + cost/weigh … each (postposed)
entries.contrast: each against every is the central distinction of this file. Each looks at members individually, one at a time; every looks at the set collectively. Each works with a set of two, every needs three or more. Each takes of and can float away from its subject; every can do neither. Almost, nearly, and practically modify every, not each — ✓ almost every day, ✗ almost each day. As a determiner each precedes a noun; standing alone it is a pronoun (Each was inspected).
entries.meaning: Picks out the members of a group one by one, treating them separately. The noun and the verb are both singular — Each student has a locker — but when each floats away from a plural subject and lands next to the verb, the verb goes back to plural: The students each have a locker, We each have our own copy. Each also survives at the end of a phrase as an adverb of price or weight: The tickets are twenty dollars each.
examples: Each student receives a locker and a combination.
Each of the four applicants was interviewed twice.
She wrote a note to each of them.
The winners each got a check for five hundred dollars.
Each day brought a new complication.
Limes are seventy-nine cents each this week.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: emphatic; natural in speech and rhetoric, and routinely cut by copy editors as redundant
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — each and every student. Never a plural (✗ each and every students), never an uncountable (✗ each and every water), exactly like both of its parts.
entries.ofRule: Not with the bare phrase — ✗ each and every of the students. The partitive is each and every one of the students, with one inserted to carry the of.
entries.pattern: each and every [singular countable noun] / each and every one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun]
entries.contrast: Semantically it adds nothing to each or to every — it is a rhetorical doubling that means "with no exceptions whatsoever, and I mean it." Grammatically it inherits every's behavior rather than each's: it cannot float (✗ The students each and every paid) and cannot take a bare of. Its counterpart at the opposite end of the register scale is the legal doublet any and all.
entries.meaning: An emphatic fusion of each and every, used when the speaker wants to insist that nothing was skipped. The verb is singular. It is common in speeches, sales pitches, and coaching talk, and because it draws attention to itself it wears out fast in writing.
examples: Each and every employee will get the same bonus this year.
I checked each and every box on that form twice.
Each and every one of you needs to sign in at the front desk.
She answers each and every email the same day.
Each and every seat in the theater was taken.
He thanked each and every volunteer by name.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, and only from a set of exactly two — either route, either parent. Never a plural (✗ either routes), never an uncountable (✗ either milk), and never a set of three or more — for three or more the word is any.
entries.ofRule: Required before a determined noun phrase or a pronoun — either of the routes, either of them. ✗ either the routes and ✗ either them are ungrammatical. Note that the noun after of is plural while the verb stays singular: Either of the plans works.
entries.pattern: either [singular countable noun] / either of [the/my/these + plural noun] / either of [them/us/you] / on either side of [noun]
entries.contrast: either is the positive dual and neither its negation: Either answer is acceptable against Neither answer is acceptable. Against any, the difference is set size — either for two, any for three or more (Either day works for a weekend, Any day works for a week). Against both, either takes one of the two where both takes them together. As a determiner either precedes a noun; standing alone it is a pronoun (Either will do), and either at the end of a negative sentence is an adverb (I don't like it either) — three different word classes for one spelling.
entries.meaning: Two distinct uses. (1) One or the other of two, it doesn't matter which — the ordinary sense: Either route gets you there. (2) Each of two, both — a fossil sense surviving in fixed spatial phrases: trees on either side of the road means both sides, not one of them. Because sense (2) is still live, either is occasionally ambiguous, and careful writers switch to each or both when they mean sense (2) anywhere other than either side, either end, either hand. The verb is singular in careful writing — Either of the plans works — though work is very common in speech.
examples: Either route will get you to the airport by six.
Either of these applicants would do the job well.
There were cornfields on either side of the highway.
I'm happy with either answer.
You can pay in cash or by card — either one is fine.
Did either of them call you back?

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — every window, every chance. Never a plural countable (✗ every windows), never an uncountable (✗ every water, ✗ every advice — for those, see every bit of). The one systematic exception is the frequency pattern, where every takes a numeral plus a plural: every three days, every ten minutes, every few weeks, every two years.
entries.ofRule: Never. ✗ every of the students does not exist in English. The repair is every one of the students for plural countables and every bit of the paint for uncountables — which is precisely why those two phrases exist.
entries.pattern: every [singular countable noun] / every [numeral] [plural time noun] (frequency) / every one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun] / almost/nearly/practically every [singular noun]
entries.contrast: every against each is the distinction to learn: every views the set collectively and wants at least three members; each views the members individually and works with two. Every takes no of and cannot float (✗ The students every arrived); each does both. Every accepts almost, nearly, and practically; each does not. Against all, every is singular where all is plural — every student was notified = all the students were notified. Against not every, note that negation is partial, not total.
entries.meaning: Covers the entire membership of a set of three or more, viewed as a complete sweep rather than as separate individuals. Both the noun and the verb are singular — Every seat is taken — but the pronoun that refers back is normally singular they in modern American usage: Every applicant should bring their own laptop. Every is the base for a whole family of emphatic and alternating phrases: every single, every last, every other, each and every.
examples: Every window on the block was broken.
She checks her email every ten minutes.
Every applicant has to submit two references.
Almost every restaurant on that street closed during the pandemic.
I've read every book he's written.
Every one of those excuses is a lie.

entries.position: central determiner heading a partitive phrase — every determines bit, and the of-phrase supplies the real noun
entries.register: neutral, mildly emphatic
entries.goesWith: uncountable nouns, reached through of — every bit of evidence, every bit of the paint, every bit of energy. It also takes a singular countable construed as a mass (every bit of that old house). Never a plural countable: ✗ every bit of the students — that is every one of the students.
entries.ofRule: Of is required; carrying the of is the entire function of bit. ✗ every bit evidence is impossible, and so is ✗ every evidence, which is why the phrase exists.
entries.pattern: every bit of [uncountable noun] / every bit of [the/my/this + uncountable noun] / every bit of [it/this/that] / every last bit of [uncountable noun]
entries.contrast: every bit of is to uncountable nouns what every one of is to plural countables: both exist because every can take neither of nor a non-singular noun. Against all of, the difference is insistence — all of the paint reports the quantity, every bit of the paint insists that none was left. Do not confuse the determiner with the adverbial every bit as (every bit as good as the original), which modifies an adjective and quantifies nothing.
entries.meaning: The partitive that lets every quantify something uncountable, insisting that the whole of it was covered with nothing left over. The verb stays singular, agreeing with bit: Every bit of the evidence was thrown out.
examples: Every bit of evidence pointed the same direction.
She used every bit of the fabric and had nothing left over.
He put every bit of energy he had into that last mile.
We scraped every bit of ice off the windshield.
Every bit of the money went to the shelter.
I meant every bit of it.

entries.respell: ev-ree-BLESS-id · blessed has two syllables here, not one — the adjective /ˈblɛsɪd/, never the past-tense /blɛst/ of he blessed the meal. The stress moves onto blessed, which is where the exasperation lives; there is no weak form, because the whole point of the word is that it is leaned on
entries.position: central determiner —
entries.register: dated, folksy, and emphatic. An American meets it in nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century fiction, in older rural and Southern speech, and from grandparents; in current writing it reads as deliberately quaint rather than wrong
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — every blessed day, every blessed one. Never a plural (✗ every blessed days), never an uncountable (✗ every blessed money), following every exactly. In practice it attaches to a short list of nouns and does not spread much beyond it: day, night, time, minute, one, thing, word, penny.
entries.pattern: every blessed [singular time noun] · every blessed one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun] · every blessed [thing/word/penny] · the whole blessed [noun] (the same intensifier in the other frame)
entries.contrast: Blessed here is a minced oath — a euphemism standing in for damned, blasted, or cursed — which is why the phrase carries irritation rather than reverence: every blessed day means "every last miserable day," not a day that was blessed. That bleaching puts it in the same family as old in any old, single in not a single, and earthly in no earthly, where an ordinary adjective has lost its meaning and kept only its force. Against every single, which counts members off, and every last, which exhausts a supply, every blessed adds exasperation and nothing else. Do not confuse it with the literal adjective in every blessed sacrament, where blessed means what it says and the phrase means what it looks like.
variants: every livelong (as in the livelong day)
entries.meaning: With of: Not with the bare phrase — ✗ every blessed of them. The partitive is every blessed one of: every blessed one of them. Emphatic every with a note of grievance in it — the speaker is complaining about the relentlessness of whatever the noun names. The noun and the verb are both singular, exactly as after plain every: Every blessed one of them was late. It has aged out of neutral American English and now works mainly as period flavor, as affectionate imitation of an older speaker, or as comic exaggeration.
examples: He calls me at six in the morning every blessed day.
She sat by that window every blessed night for a year.
We spent every blessed penny we had on the roof.
Every blessed one of those forms had to be signed twice.
"I've told you every blessed thing I know," he said, and shut the door. — the phrase as fiction sets it down
The machine broke down every blessed time we ran it.
Current American writing says every single day here; every blessed day is the grandparent's version of the same sentence. — the register in one line

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: informal and emphatic — common in speech, rare in formal writing
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — every last dime, every last crumb. Never a plural (✗ every last dimes), never an uncountable (✗ every last money), following every exactly.
entries.ofRule: Not with the bare phrase. Use every last one of for countables — every last one of them — and every last bit of for uncountables.
entries.pattern: every last [singular countable noun] / every last one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun] / every last bit of [uncountable noun]
entries.contrast: every last and every single are near-twins; every last leans toward the exhaustion of a supply (every last dollar, every last drop), while every single leans toward counting off members of a set (every single person in the room). To reach an uncountable noun, both need a partitive: every last bit of the paint.
entries.meaning: Emphatic every, insisting that the set has been used up or accounted for down to the final member. It carries a note of effort or grievance — the speaker is usually pointing out that this took some doing, or that nothing was left over.
examples: He spent every last dime of his savings on that truck.
We ate every last crumb of the cake.
She read every last page of the contract before signing it.
They fired every last one of us.
I want every last box out of this garage by Sunday.
The drought killed every last seedling in the field.

entries.position: central determiner heading its own partitive phrase — the head of the phrase is one, not the plural noun after of
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: of plus a plural noun that already has a determiner, or a pronoun — every one of the students, every one of my cousins, every one of them. Never a bare plural (✗ every one of students), never an uncountable (✗ every one of the water — that is all of the water or every bit of the water).
entries.ofRule: Of is required — that is the whole point of the phrase. Every itself cannot take of, so one is inserted to carry it.
entries.pattern: every one of [the/these/my + plural noun] / every one of [them/us/you] / every single one of … / every last one of …
entries.contrast: The trap is spelling. Every one (two words) is this partitive determiner and refers to things or people already specified: Every one of the cookies was gone. Everyone (one word) is an indefinite pronoun, refers only to people, and never takes of: Everyone laughed. If you can insert single between the words, it is two words. Against all of, this phrase counts the members one at a time and takes a singular verb, where all of takes them as a body and agrees with the noun.
entries.meaning: The repair phrase that lets every do what every alone cannot: attach to a noun phrase that already has a determiner. The verb stays singular — Every one of the applicants was rejected — which is the giveaway that the head of the phrase is one.
examples: Every one of the applicants was rejected.
I've met every one of her brothers.
Every one of them denied knowing anything about it.
She corrected every one of my mistakes in red ink.
Every one of those windows needs to be replaced.
Every single one of the tickets sold in under an hour.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — every other week, every other student. Never a plural (✗ every other weeks), never an uncountable, inheriting every's restriction exactly.
entries.ofRule: Not with the bare phrase. Every other one of exists but is clumsy and is usually rephrased as every second one.
entries.pattern: every other [singular time noun] (alternating) / every other [singular countable noun] (the remainder) / every second [time noun] (synonym of the alternating sense)
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with each other, which is a reciprocal pronoun, not a determiner: They helped each other means mutually, and every other never means that. Within every other itself, the noun tells the two senses apart: a time noun gives the alternating reading (every other Tuesday), and any other noun in a context of comparison gives the remainder reading (every other candidate withdrew). Its negative and free-choice twins are no other and any other.
entries.meaning: Two distinct uses. (1) Alternating — every second one, skipping one in between: We meet every other Thursday means twice a month, on alternate Thursdays. (2) All the remaining ones, everything apart from the one just named: Every other option was worse means all the rest were worse. Sense (2) is what makes comparative sentences work — She's faster than every other runner on the team correctly excludes her from the comparison class, where than every runner would absurdly include her.
examples: The recycling truck comes every other Tuesday.
She calls her mother every other day.
Every other candidate had already withdrawn by March.
He's cheaper than every other contractor we called.
They repainted every other room and left the rest.
Every other seat was blocked off for distancing.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: informal to neutral, emphatic
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — every single person, every single time. Never a plural (✗ every single people), never an uncountable (✗ every single information).
entries.ofRule: Not with the bare phrase. Use every single one of — every single one of them.
entries.pattern: every single [singular countable noun] / every single one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun] / every single time [clause]
entries.contrast: Every single counts off members and stresses that not one was missed; every last stresses that a supply was used up; each and every is the third member of the emphatic set and the most formal-sounding of the three, which is why it turns up in speeches. All three take a singular noun and a singular verb. The negative mirror image is not a single.
entries.meaning: Emphatic every, adding "with no exceptions at all." It is the most common emphatic determiner in spoken American English, and every single time has become a near-idiom for expressing exasperation at something predictable.
examples: Every single person in the room turned around.
He forgets his badge every single time.
I read every single review before I bought it.
Every single one of those files was corrupted.
She's been late every single day this month.
They checked every single seat for the missing ring.

entries.term: every third / every fourth / every nth
entries.respell: ev-ree-THURD, ev-ree-FORTH, ev-ree-ENTH · the stress moves onto the ordinal, which carries the whole meaning and therefore has no weak form; every keeps its ordinary two-syllable /ˈɛvri/ and does reduce, to [ˌɛvri] or even [ˌɛvi], since it is the unstressed half. The final clusters simplify in speech: every fifth row → [ˌɛvri ˈfɪf roʊ], every sixth one → [ˌɛvri ˈsɪks wʌn]
entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral; the nth form is informal in speech and technical in writing
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — every third row, every fourth patient, every tenth customer. Never a plural after the ordinal (✗ every third rows), never an uncountable (✗ every third water), inheriting every's restriction exactly. Do not confuse it with the frequency pattern, which takes a cardinal plus a plural: every three days, every ten minutes. The two are the same interval expressed two ways, and each has its own number agreement.
entries.pattern: every [ordinal] + [singular countable noun] · every [cardinal] + [plural time noun] (the frequency twin: every three days) · every nth [noun] (unspecified interval) · every third one of … (grammatical, avoided)
entries.contrast: Two patterns sit side by side and mean the same thing with opposite grammar: every third day (ordinal + singular) and every three days (cardinal + plural). Both name an interval of three, and crossing them produces ✗ every third days and ✗ every three day. Against every other in its alternating sense, this is the same construction with the gap widened — every other week is every second week, and from three up the ordinal series takes over: every third week, every fourth week. Watch how the interval is counted: every third row means rows one, four, and seven — two rows skipped, not three — which is the same inclusive counting that makes every other skip only one. Every nth is the algebraist's placeholder let loose in ordinary speech, where it usually means "at some regular interval I am not going to specify."
entries.meaning: With of: Not with the bare phrase — ✗ every third of the rows, inheriting every's prohibition. Every third one of the rows is grammatical and clumsy, and Americans rewrite it as one in three of the rows or a third of the rows. Names a repeating interval by counting positions in a series. The noun and the verb are both singular — Every fourth seat is blocked off — exactly as with plain every. It is the workhorse pattern of schedules, sampling plans, seating charts, and quality control, and it runs indefinitely up the ordinal series, which is why nth exists as an informal cover term for the whole family.
examples: Every third row of seats was left empty.
The inspector pulls every fourth unit off the line and tests it. — quality control
She works every third weekend, so we plan around it.
Every fifth customer gets a free coffee. — a promotion
Plant them six inches apart and stake every sixth one. — an instruction
He tells that same story every nth time we go out, and I still laugh.
Every third day and every three days mean the same thing — ordinal with a singular, cardinal with a plural.

entries.position: central determiner in form, but frozen — the phrase behaves as a single lexical item, not as a productive pattern
entries.register: informal idiom; fine in speech and casual writing, out of place in formal prose
entries.goesWith: the singular countable noun way, and effectively nothing else — every which way. Every which direction is occasionally heard; beyond that the phrase does not extend (✗ every which chair, ✗ every which student). Learn it as one word-sized chunk rather than as a rule.
entries.ofRule: Never — ✗ every which of the ways.
entries.pattern: [verb of scattering or turning] + every which way / going/running/flying every which way / every which way but loose
entries.contrast: It looks like two central determiners stacked — every on top of which — and historically that is what it was, but modern English allows only one central determiner per noun phrase, which is exactly why the phrase cannot be extended to a new noun. Against plain every way, which means "by all available means" (we tried every way we could), every which way means "in all directions at once, with no order to it." The disorder is part of the meaning. Its free-choice twin is any which way ("in whatever direction, it doesn't matter which") — the same fossil with any swapped in for every.
entries.meaning: A fossilized emphatic meaning "in every direction, all over the place." The noun phrase functions adverbially, so it normally answers where or how rather than serving as a subject or object.
examples: The wind sent the leaflets every which way.
Kids were running every which way across the parking lot.
His notes go every which way on the page.
When the alarm went off, people scattered every which way.
The old fence posts lean every which way.
She turned the map every which way and still got lost.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (any questions) and uncountable nouns (any money) in questions, negatives, and conditionals; singular countable nouns in the free-choice sense (any student can tell you) and with a small set of abstract nouns (any idea, any reason, any chance, any doubt, any way). Not an ordinary singular countable in plain polarity use: ✗ Did you buy any apple? — say any apples.
entries.ofRule: Required before a determined noun phrase or a pronoun — any of the students, any of this money, any of them. ✗ any the students is ungrammatical. Bare any + noun takes no of.
entries.pattern: Do you have any [plural/uncountable noun]? / [negated verb] + any [plural/uncountable noun] / if … any [noun] / any [singular countable noun] (free choice) / any of [the/my + noun or pronoun]
entries.contrast: any against some is a matter of polarity, not of meaning. Some is the default in affirmative statements (I bought some apples); any is the default in negatives and open questions (I didn't buy any apples, Did you buy any apples?). The exception that trips learners is the polite offer: a question that expects or invites a yes takes some, not any — Would you like some coffee?, Could you lend me some cash? Would you like any coffee? is grammatical but sounds grudging, as if you would rather not pour it. Against no, the two are alternative ways of negating and never co-occur: ✓ I have no money, ✓ I don't have any money, ✗ I have no any money. Against either, the difference is set size — either for exactly two, any for three or more. As a determiner any precedes a noun; standing alone it is a pronoun (Is there any left?).
entries.meaning: Two distinct uses. (1) Negative polarity — in questions, negatives, conditionals, and after negative-flavored words (hardly, rarely, without, refuse, doubt, before), any marks a quantity whose existence is open or denied: Do you have any questions?, He left without any explanation. (2) Free choice — in affirmative statements, any takes a singular countable noun and means "it doesn't matter which one": Any mechanic can fix that. Sense (2) is not a negative at all, and it is the one that surprises learners taught that "any is for negatives." Stress separates them in speech: free-choice any is stressed, polarity any is not. After of + plural, the verb may be singular or plural — If any of the files is/are missing, tell me.
examples: Do you have any questions before we start?
We didn't get any warning that the road was closed.
Did you bring any cash, or should I stop at an ATM?
Any student can tell you that class is a waste of time.
If any of these numbers look wrong, flag them.
He left without any explanation at all.
Is there any chance you could come in on Saturday?
Take any seat you like.
related: any manner of / any kind of / any sort of

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: legal and contractual boilerplate; in ordinary prose it reads as padding
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (any and all claims, any and all documents) and uncountable nouns (any and all liability, any and all correspondence). Never a singular countable: ✗ any and all claim.
entries.ofRule: Possible but heavy — any and all of the documents. Contracts normally write any and all documents instead and keep the of out of it.
entries.pattern: any and all [plural countable noun] / any and all [uncountable noun] / waive/deny any and all [rights/claims/liability]
entries.contrast: Semantically it is just all, with any prefixed to close the loophole that a reader might argue all covers only the items already listed. Legal drafters keep it for that belt-and-suspenders reason; plain-language style guides delete it. It is the mirror image of each and every — the same doubling instinct at the opposite end of the register scale.
entries.meaning: An emphatic legal doublet meaning "every one of these, without exception and however described." Its job is to defeat a narrow reading, which is why it clusters around claims, rights, liability, damages, and documents. Outside contracts and formal notices it sounds like someone imitating a lawyer.
examples: The tenant waives any and all claims against the landlord.
Please produce any and all correspondence relating to the sale.
The company denies any and all liability for the delay.
Any and all unused funds revert to the general account.
She is authorized to sign any and all documents on his behalf.
The release covers any and all injuries arising from the event.

entries.term: any manner of / any kind of / any sort of
entries.ipa: /ˌɛni ˈmænɚ əv/, /ˌɛni ˈkaɪnd əv/, /ˌɛni ˈsɔrt əv/
entries.respell: en-ee-MAN-ur-uv, en-ee-KYND-uv, en-ee-SORT-uv · the stress sits on manner, kind, or sort, and of takes its weak form /əv/ and regularly reduces to /ə/, giving [ˈmænɚə], [ˈkaɪndə], and — with the flapped /t/ — [ˈsɔrɾə]. Any has two weak forms here, and they separate the two senses: polarity any is unstressed and reduces toward [əni], so not any kind of proof runs to [nɑɾ əni ˈkaɪndə ˈpruf], while free-choice any is stressed and keeps its full [ˈɛni]. The casual reductions kinda and sorta belong to the hedging adverb (kinda tired), never here, where the of is structural and the phrase keeps its shape
entries.type: quantifier (negative-polarity and free choice, partitive, category-covering)
entries.position: any is the central determiner of a partitive phrase whose head is manner, kind, or sort; the of-phrase supplies the real noun
entries.register: any kind of and any sort of are neutral to informal and entirely ordinary in American speech; any manner of is formal and archaic-flavored. An American meets any manner of in contracts, leases, insurance policies, older statutes, and the King James Bible, and essentially never in conversation, where it would sound like someone doing an impression of a deed
entries.goesWith: uncountable nouns (any manner of doubt, any kind of proof) and plural countable nouns (any manner of alterations, any sort of guarantees), reached through of. A singular countable works only with its article left in place after of — any kind of a plan — and that pattern is informal and usually edited out. Note the fossilized singular inside the phrase: ✗ any manners of work, ✗ any kinds of proof, even though manners and kinds are perfectly good nouns elsewhere.
entries.ofRule: Of is required and is part of the phrase — ✗ any manner doubt, ✗ any kind proof. No determiner may follow it: ✓ any manner of excuses, ✗ any manner of the excuses. To select from a set already identified, drop the frame and use plain any of: any of those excuses.
entries.pattern: [negated verb] + any manner of [uncountable/plural noun] · without any kind of [noun] · if any sort of [noun] · any kind of [noun] will do (free choice) · any kind of a [singular noun] (informal) · Is that any kind of [noun]? (the dismissive question)
entries.contrast: This is the polarity partner of no manner of / no kind of / no sort of, and the pair splits exactly as any and no do: there was no manner of doubt puts the negative on the determiner, there wasn't any manner of doubt puts it on the verb, and the two mean the same thing. They never combine: ✗ no any manner of doubt. Like plain any, it has two senses — negative-polarity in questions, negatives, and conditionals (without any kind of warning), and free choice in affirmatives (any kind of wrench will do) — and stress tells them apart. Against all manner of, which is affirmative and exhaustive ("every variety there is"), this frame is open ("whichever variety, or none"): all manner of excuses says he produced many, any kind of excuse says one would do. Against any such, which is anaphoric and reaches back to the one thing just described, this covers a whole category and needs no antecedent. And keep the dismissive question apart from the quantifying use: Is that any kind of apology? judges quality, not quantity.
variants: all kinds of / all sorts of
entries.meaning: Holds open a whole category rather than a quantity — "anything of that description, in any form at all." Kind and sort are the everyday words and manner the ceremonial one; the three are otherwise interchangeable, and only manner carries the archaic flavor. The verb agrees with the noun after of rather than with manner — If any manner of records survive, the archive has not found them — though the agreement is as unsettled here as in the negative twin, and careful writers rebuild the sentence rather than decide.
examples: The lease does not permit any manner of alterations without written consent. — contract boilerplate, where manner still lives
Ye shall not do any manner of work therein. — the King James sabbath formula, and the reason the phrase still sounds biblical
There wasn't any manner of doubt that the signature was genuine. — the negation on the verb; there was no manner of doubt puts it on the determiner instead
They never offered any kind of explanation for the delay.
The used dryer came without any sort of guarantee.
Bring any kind of dish you like — it's a potluck. — free choice, stressed, in ordinary speech
✗ They didn't offer any manner of the explanations. — impossible; no determiner may follow the of. Say any of those explanations.
related: no manner of / no kind of / no sort of
all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.position: central determiner — any fills the determiner slot and old is a fixed intensifier with no reference to age
entries.register: informal and colloquial; ordinary in speech, out of place in formal writing
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns (any old excuse), plural countable nouns (any old boxes), and uncountable nouns (any old junk) — the same range as free-choice any, though it is most at home with a singular countable.
entries.ofRule: Not used — ✗ any old of them. The partitive is plain any of them.
entries.pattern: any old [noun] / not just any old [noun] / any old time / any old thing / any old how
entries.contrast: old here is a dismissive intensifier, not an adjective of age: any old chair does not mean an aged chair, it means "whatever chair, I don't care which," and it works fine for a chair fresh out of the box. The negated frame not just any old flips the sense into praise — That's not just any old guitar means it is special. Against plain any, the difference is attitude rather than grammar: any is neutral free choice, any old adds a shrug.
entries.meaning: Colloquial free choice with a shrug — the speaker is signaling that the choice does not matter and that the standard is low. Because old has bleached out of its literal meaning, it attaches happily to brand-new things without contradiction.
examples: Grab any old chair; it doesn't matter which one.
He'll eat any old thing you put in front of him.
Come by any old time this weekend.
That's not just any old guitar — it belonged to her father.
You can't just throw any old numbers into the spreadsheet.
She keeps any old junk that might come in handy someday.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns (any other question), plural countable nouns (any other questions), and uncountable nouns (any other evidence) — it inherits the full range of any.
entries.ofRule: any other of the applicants is grammatical but stiff; Americans reorder it to any of the other applicants, where of attaches to any and is required.
entries.pattern: any other [noun] / [comparative] + than any other [singular countable noun] / before/without any other [noun]
entries.contrast: The comparative trap is why this phrase earns its own entry. She is faster than any other runner on the team is correct because other subtracts her from the set she is compared against; She is faster than any runner on the team is illogical, since it claims she is faster than herself. The same repair applies with no other — No other city has this problem excludes the city under discussion. Its universal twin is every other in that word's remainder sense.
entries.meaning: Points to a member of the set outside the one already named. In comparisons it is doing real logical work rather than merely adding a word: other subtracts the subject from the comparison class.
examples: Chicago has colder winters than any other big American city.
Do you have any other questions for the panel?
He wouldn't accept help from any other doctor.
There wasn't any other evidence to go on.
She'd rather live here than in any other state.
Call me if any other problems come up.

entries.respell: en-ee-SUCH · such keeps its full vowel /sʌtʃ/ and the stress, exactly as in no such and unlike the weak such a [sətʃə] of the exclamative. Polarity any is unstressed in front of it and reduces toward [əni], so the phrase lands as [əni ˈsʌtʃ]; free-choice any such keeps the fuller [ˈɛni ˈsʌtʃ]
entries.register: neutral, leaning formal — its natural home is legal, official, and academic prose
entries.goesWith: all three noun types, exactly like any — singular countable (any such claim, any such person), plural countable (any such records, any such payments), and uncountable (any such evidence, any such conduct). The singular countable takes no article: ✓ any such request, ✗ any such a request.
entries.pattern: if any such [noun] exists · [negated verb] + any such [noun] · without any such [noun] · deny/dispute any such [noun] · Any such [noun] shall be … (the contract frame)
entries.contrast: any such is the polarity partner of no such, and the pair splits exactly as any and no do: no such rule exists puts the negative on the determiner, there isn't any such rule puts it on the verb, and the two mean the same thing. They never combine: ✗ no any such rule. What such adds to any is anaphora — any rule denies rules in general, any such rule denies the particular rule just described, so the phrase needs a description already on the table. And note the article rule it shares with no such and breaks with such a, such an: such a mess keeps the article, any such mess drops it, because any has already spent the slot.
entries.meaning: With of: Not with the bare phrase — ✗ any such of the claims, ✗ any such of them, inheriting the block that such puts on the partitive. To reach an already-identified set, drop such and use plain any of: any of those claims. Any such one exists and is stilted. Denies or holds open the existence of anything of the kind just mentioned. It is anaphoric — such points back at a description already given — and it is the shape the negative takes when the negation lands on the verb instead of on the determiner. Contracts and statutes lean on it because it lets a clause reach back to a defined term without repeating it: any such notice means "any notice of the kind defined above." The verb agrees with the noun after it: Any such record is confidential, Any such records are confidential. The determiners that reduce a set to zero — plus the two that reduce it only partway, and the rules that keep English from stacking two negatives in one clause. Related negatives of small quantity (hardly any, scarcely any, barely any, next to no, a shred of) are in quantifiers of small quantity; the dialectal and archaic negatives — ain't no, ary / ary a, nary a, never a, and negative concord — have their own section below. One phrase that looks as though it belongs in this section does not. An absence of is not a determiner at all but a full lexical noun heading its own noun phrase: it takes the and a possessive (the absence of evidence, in his absence), it pluralizes (three unexplained absences), it accepts modifiers (a complete absence of, a conspicuous absence of), and — the decisive test — the verb agrees with absence rather than with the noun after of: ✓ An absence of witnesses was noted, ✗ were noted. In a genuine partitive determiner like every bit of or a shred of, the of-phrase supplies the real noun; here it does not. To deny a quantity, the determiners are no and none of; to name the smallest imaginable amount and then deny even that, see a shred of and not so much as a.
examples: If any such records still exist, the archive has not found them.
The company denies that any such agreement was ever reached.
There is no evidence of any such payment anywhere in the ledger.
Any such request must be submitted in writing within thirty days. — the standard contract frame
He left without any such explanation, and nobody asked for one.
I've never heard of any such rule, and I've read the handbook twice.
✗ Do you have any such a form? — nonstandard; any has already filled the determiner slot, so drop the a.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral, slightly formal — everyday speech often prefers not either or neither one
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, and only from a set of exactly two — neither candidate, neither parent. Never a plural (✗ neither candidates), never an uncountable (✗ neither milk), and never a set of three or more — for three or more the words are no and none of.
entries.ofRule: Required before a determined phrase or a pronoun — neither of the candidates, neither of them. ✗ neither the candidates and ✗ neither them are ungrammatical. The noun after of is plural while the verb stays singular: Neither of the plans works.
entries.pattern: neither [singular countable noun] / neither of [the/my/these + plural noun] / neither of [them/us/you] / neither one of [them]
entries.contrast: neither is the negation of either and covers exactly two: Neither answer is right. For three or more, use none of the answers or no answer. Because neither is already negative it cannot sit in a clause that is negated again — ✗ I don't like neither of them is nonstandard; write I don't like either of them or I like neither of them. As a determiner neither precedes a noun; standing alone it is a pronoun (Neither will do), and Neither do I is an adverbial construction with subject–verb inversion.
entries.meaning: Denies both members of a two-member set at once: not the one and not the other. The noun and the verb are both singular — Neither candidate was available — and in careful writing the verb stays singular even after of + plural: Neither of the plans works. Plural agreement (Neither of the plans work) is very common in speech and increasingly in print, but the singular remains the safe choice in edited prose.
examples: Neither candidate answered the question.
Neither of my parents finished college.
She liked neither option, so we started over.
Neither of them has called back.
Neither road is plowed yet.
Neither one of those explanations makes sense.

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral; in subject position it is the only option, and elsewhere it is the more emphatic and more written choice
entries.goesWith: all three noun types — singular countable (no answer), plural countable (no answers), and uncountable (no time). It is one of the very few determiners with no countability restriction at all. It cannot follow another central determiner: ✗ the no answer, ✗ my no money.
entries.ofRule: Never. ✗ no of the students does not exist. The partitive is none of the students — which is the entire reason none of is a separate headword.
entries.pattern: no [singular countable noun] / no [plural countable noun] / no [uncountable noun] / There is/are no [noun] / No [noun] + verb (subject position)
entries.contrast: no against not any is a choice of position and force, not of meaning: We found no survivors = We didn't find any survivors. No is stronger, and it is required when the negated phrase is the subject — ✓ No students came, ✗ Not any students came. Against none, the split is grammatical: no precedes a noun, none stands alone or takes of — ✓ No tickets are left / ✓ None are left / ✓ None of the tickets are left / ✗ No of the tickets are left. Against neither, no has no limit on set size while neither is confined to two. Against not all, no is total negation where not all is partial.
variants: no way / no doubt / no idea (fixed phrases)
entries.meaning: Reduces the noun to zero. The verb agrees with the noun that follows, not with no — No student was notified, No students were notified, No news is good news. Because no is itself the negative it never combines with another negative in the same clause: ✗ I have no any money is impossible in every variety of English, and I don't have no money is negative concord — systematic in several American dialects but nonstandard in edited writing. No is also the base of a large set of fixed phrases: no doubt, no way, no idea, no problem, no such thing, no wonder.
examples: There is no excuse for that email.
No students signed up for the eight o'clock section.
We have no time to argue about it.
No two witnesses told the same story.
She had no idea he was already gone.
No news is good news.
There's no way I'm driving in this.

entries.respell: noh-URTH-lee · the stress moves onto earthly. Neither word has a weak form — no carries the clause's negation and keeps its full diphthong, and earthly is the emphatic the phrase exists for; many Americans voice the /θ/ to [ð], giving [ˈɚðli], and the whole phrase runs to [noʊ ˈɚðli] with no break
entries.position: central determiner —
entries.register: emphatic, informal to neutral; slightly old-fashioned but in current American use, and heard most in the fixed phrases no earthly idea and no earthly reason
entries.goesWith: a short list of singular countable abstract nouns — no earthly idea, no earthly reason, no earthly use, no earthly chance, no earthly way, no earthly clue. It does not extend freely to concrete nouns: ✗ no earthly chair, ✗ no earthly student. A plural is possible but rare (no earthly reasons), and it reaches an uncountable only in the fossil no earthly good (it did him no earthly good).
entries.pattern: have no earthly [idea/clue/reason] · There is no earthly [reason/way] to [verb] · do someone no earthly good · of no earthly use (to someone) · what earthly [noun] …? (the same intensifier in a question)
entries.contrast: Earthly is a bleached intensifier, not an adjective of place: no earthly reason does not contrast a terrestrial reason with a heavenly one, it means "no reason whatsoever." The literal adjective is the one in earthly possessions and earthly delights, and it is a different word doing a different job. The bleaching puts this phrase with old in any old, single in not a single, and blessed in every blessed. Against plain no the difference is force alone — I have no idea reports, I have no earthly idea insists — and against the postposed emphasizers no idea whatsoever and no idea at all, which sharpen the same negative from the other end of the phrase, the difference is only position; see whatsoever.
variants: not the faintest / not the foggiest
entries.meaning: With of: Never — ✗ no earthly of them, ✗ no earthly of the reasons, inheriting no's prohibition exactly. The partitive is none of: none of it was any earthly use. An emphatic no meaning "none at all, none even conceivable." It comes from an older habit of swearing by heaven and earth, and the same idea survives with the phrase moved behind the noun — no reason on earth — which is the version most Americans now reach for. The verb agrees with the noun, exactly as after no: No earthly reason exists for that clause. Learn it as a short list of collocations rather than as a productive rule, because it does not spread past them.
examples: I have no earthly idea where he put the keys.
There's no earthly reason to drive all the way out there tonight.
That contraption is of no earthly use to anybody.
She had no earthly clue the meeting had been moved. — informal speech, where the phrase is commonest
It did him no earthly good to argue with the inspector. — the uncountable fossil
What earthly reason could she have for lying about it? — the same intensifier in a question, with the negation carried by the rhetorical frame
No reason on earth says the same thing with the phrase behind the noun.

entries.term: no manner of / no kind of / no sort of
entries.ipa: /ˌnoʊ ˈmænɚ əv/, /ˌnoʊ ˈkaɪnd əv/, /ˌnoʊ ˈsɔrt əv/
entries.respell: noh-MAN-ur-uv, noh-KYND-uv, noh-SORT-uv · of takes its weak form /əv/ and regularly reduces to /ə/, giving [ˈmænɚə], [ˈkaɪndə], and — with the flapped /t/ — [ˈsɔrɾə]; no has no weak form, since it carries the clause's negation. The casual reductions kinda and sorta belong to the hedging adverb (kinda tired), not here, where the of is structural and the phrase keeps its shape
entries.register: no kind of and no sort of are neutral to informal; no manner of is formal and archaic-flavored. An American meets no manner of in contracts and older statutes and, above all, in the King James Bible, where no manner of work is the sabbath formula — which is why the phrase still sounds biblical in anyone's mouth
entries.goesWith: uncountable nouns (no manner of doubt, no kind of proof) and plural countable nouns (no manner of excuses, no sort of guarantees), reached through of. A singular countable works only with its article left in place after of — no sort of a plan — and that pattern is informal and usually edited out. Note the fossilized singular inside the phrase: ✗ no manners of work, ✗ no kinds of proof, even though manners and kinds are perfectly good nouns elsewhere.
entries.pattern: no manner of [uncountable/plural noun] · no kind of [noun] · no sort of a [singular noun] (informal) · That's no kind of [noun] (predicative, dismissive) · not … any manner of [noun] (the polarity twin)
entries.contrast: All three deny not just the thing but every variety of it: no proof denies proof, no kind of proof denies proof of any description. They are the negative counterpart of all manner of and all kinds of, all sorts of, which sit with the predeterminers, and the polarity partner of any manner of — there wasn't any manner of doubt puts the negation on the verb, there was no manner of doubt puts it on the determiner, and the two mean the same thing. As always, they never combine: ✗ no any manner of doubt. Against no such, which is anaphoric and denies the one thing just described, these deny a whole category and need no antecedent. And keep the dismissive predicative use apart from the quantifying one: That's no kind of apology judges quality, not quantity.
variants: all kinds of / all sorts of
entries.meaning: With of: Of is required and is part of the phrase — ✗ no manner doubt, ✗ no kind proof. No determiner may follow it: ✓ no manner of excuses, ✗ no manner of the excuses. To select from a set already identified, switch to the real partitive none of: none of the excuses. Denies a category outright — "nothing of that description, in any form at all." Kind and sort are the everyday words and manner the ceremonial one; the three are otherwise interchangeable, and only manner carries the archaic flavor. The verb agrees with the noun after of rather than with manner — No manner of excuses were accepted — though the agreement is genuinely unsettled here and careful writers tend to rebuild the sentence rather than decide. The dismissive predicative use (that's no kind of answer) has drifted from quantity into judgment and is by far the liveliest use of the frame in American speech.
examples: There is no manner of doubt that the signature is genuine. — formal writing, where manner still lives
No manner of work shall be done on that day. — the King James formula, and the reason the phrase sounds biblical
They offered no kind of explanation for the delay.
No sort of guarantee came with the used dryer.
That's no kind of apology, and you know it. — the dismissive use, the commonest live one
The lease permits no manner of alterations without written consent. — contract boilerplate
✗ There was no any manner of doubt. — impossible; no and any are two candidates for one slot. Say no manner of doubt or not any manner of doubt.
related: any manner of / any kind of / any sort of
all kinds of, all sorts of

entries.position: central determiner
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: all three noun types, like no — singular countable (no other choice), plural countable (no other options), and uncountable (no other evidence).
entries.ofRule: Never — no takes no of-phrase of any kind. The partitive is none of the other — none of the other applicants.
entries.pattern: no other [noun] / There is no other [noun] / No other [noun] + verb (subject position) / have no other choice but to [verb]
entries.contrast: It is the negative twin of any other and does the same logical job in comparisons: No other city has this problem excludes the city being discussed. Written as No city has this problem, the sentence would contradict itself. The fixed phrase no other choice competes with no choice — no other choice implies one option remains, no choice implies none does.
entries.meaning: Excludes every member of the set except the one already named. It shows up constantly in superlative claims and in advertising, where no other does the work of a superlative without having to prove one.
examples: No other airline flies from here to Boise nonstop.
She had no other choice but to sell the house.
No other candidate came close in the primary.
There was no other evidence tying him to the scene.
No other product on the market does all three things.
We looked, but no other apartments in that range were available.

entries.position: no is the central determiner; such follows it as a pre-head modifier inside the same phrase. Because no has already taken the one central-determiner slot English allows, there is no room left for an article: ✗ no such a thing, ✗ the no such rule
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: all three noun types, exactly like no — singular countable (no such thing, no such person), plural countable (no such rules, no such records), and uncountable (no such evidence, no such luck). The singular countable takes no article: ✓ no such thing, ✗ no such a thing.
entries.ofRule: Never — ✗ no such of the rules, ✗ no such of them, inheriting no's prohibition exactly. To reach an already-identified set, switch to none of (none of those rules) or to the fixed phrase nothing of the sort.
entries.pattern: There is no such [singular countable noun] / no such [plural countable / uncountable noun] / no such thing as [noun phrase] / No such [noun] + verb (subject position)
entries.contrast: The article rule is the whole trap. Such a, such an requires the article with a singular countable — such a mess — but no such drops it, because no and a are competing for one slot: ✓ no such thing, ✗ no such a thing (occasionally heard in speech and found in older writing, but nonstandard in edited American English). Against plain no, such adds anaphora: no rule exists denies rules in general, no such rule exists denies the particular rule just described. Against no other, the two point opposite ways — no other excludes everything except the one named, no such excludes the one named itself.
entries.meaning: Denies that anything of the kind just mentioned exists. It is anaphoric — it needs a description already on the table, and such points back at it. The verb agrees with the noun that follows, exactly as after no: No such rule exists, No such rules exist. Two of its fixed phrases have hardened into idiom: no such thing as introduces what is being denied, and No such luck is a stock reply meaning the hoped-for outcome did not arrive.
examples: There is no such thing as a free lunch.
No such rule appears anywhere in the handbook.
We checked the roster twice and found no such person.
No such records were kept before 1974.
The report offered no such evidence.
I was hoping the meeting would be canceled — no such luck.
✗ There's no such a thing as a free lunch. — nonstandard in American English; no has already filled the determiner slot, so drop the a.

entries.position: not a central determiner in the ordinary sense — none is a pronoun heading its own phrase and the of-phrase supplies the noun, which is exactly why ✗ none students fails
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: of plus a noun phrase that is already definite, or a pronoun — a plural countable (none of the students), an uncountable (none of the money), or a pronoun (none of them). Never directly before a bare noun: ✗ none students, ✗ none money — those are no students and no money.
entries.ofRule: Of is required. Without it, none is a bare pronoun standing alone (How many survived? None.) and cannot take a noun at all.
entries.pattern: none of [the/these/my + plural noun] / none of [the/this + uncountable noun] / none of [them/us/it] / none of the above
entries.contrast: No and none split the work of one meaning: no attaches directly to a noun, none stands alone or takes of. ✓ No tickets are left / ✓ None are left / ✓ None of the tickets are left / ✗ No of the tickets are left. Against neither of, the difference is set size — neither of covers exactly two, none of covers three or more. Against not any of, the two are near-equivalents, but none of is the one that works comfortably as the subject of a sentence.
entries.meaning: Denies every member of an already-identified group. The verb may be singular or plural when the noun after of is plural, and both are fully standard — None of the files was saved and None of the files were saved are equally correct, with the plural far more common in American usage. The old rule that none must be singular because it means "not one" is a nineteenth-century invention with no basis in the history of the word. With an uncountable noun the verb is singular: None of the money is missing.
examples: None of the students turned in the assignment.
None of the money was ever recovered.
I called three times and none of them picked up.
None of this makes any sense to me.
None of the above applies to part-time employees.
Honestly, none of your explanations add up.

entries.position: not negates the phrase and sits in front of the central determiner a/an
entries.register: emphatic; neutral inside fixed phrases like not a chance, not a soul
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, since a/an itself takes only a singular countable — not a word, not an excuse. For a plural or an uncountable the phrase is not any or no: ✗ not a students, ✗ not a money.
entries.ofRule: Not directly — ✗ not a of them. The partitive routes are not a single one of the students and not one of the students.
entries.pattern: Not a [singular countable noun] + singular verb / not an [noun beginning with a vowel sound] / There wasn't a [noun] / [subject] didn't [verb] a [noun]
entries.contrast: Against plain no, not a is more emphatic and more countable-flavored: There was no chair in the room states a fact, There wasn't a chair in the room insists on the count. Against not one and not a single, not a is the mildest of the three. Note the position rule: fronted before a subject, not a stays intact and sounds literary (Not a sound was heard); after the verb, the negative normally migrates onto the auxiliary and the noun phrase keeps only the bare article (There wasn't a sound). Both are the same construction.
variants: not a chance / not a soul (fixed phrases)
entries.meaning: Negates the indefinite article, insisting that not even one instance exists. Two positions are available and they are not equally common. Fronted, before the subject, the negative stays attached to the noun phrase. After the verb, the negative moves onto the auxiliary and the article is left behind — which is the ordinary spoken form, and still the same construction underneath.
examples: Not a soul was out on the street at that hour.
Not an hour goes by that I don't think about it.
Not a dime of that money ever reached the charity.
Not a word of this leaves the room.
There wasn't a cloud in the sky all week. — the same construction with the negative moved onto the verb
He didn't say a word to me the entire drive home. — negative on the verb again

entries.position: not negates the phrase; a is the central determiner and single an emphatic adjective inside it
entries.register: emphatic — never a plain statement of fact, always a point being made
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, because the phrase contains a — not a single seat, not a single complaint. Never a plural (✗ not a single seats), never an uncountable (✗ not a single money — say not a single dollar, or no money).
entries.ofRule: Through one — not a single one of the students, not a single one of them. ✗ not a single of them is ungrammatical.
entries.pattern: Not a single [singular countable noun] + singular verb / There wasn't a single [noun] / not a single one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun]
entries.contrast: This is the top of the zero-quantity scale, which runs not any (plain) → no (firmer) → not a (emphatic) → not one / not a single (most emphatic). Not a single and not one are interchangeable, with not a single a shade more colloquial. Single here is purely an intensifier — it has nothing to do with being unmarried or one-part — and it is the same intensifier that makes every single.
entries.meaning: Counts the set down to zero and dares the hearer to find an exception. The verb is singular even when the of-phrase after it is plural: Not a single one of the machines was working.
examples: Not a single seat was left by the time we got there.
In four years she missed not a single practice.
Not a single one of the applicants had the certification.
Not a single person complained about the change.
He read the contract twice and found not a single error.
There wasn't a single light on in the whole building.

entries.position: not negates the predeterminer all, and the whole phrase occupies the predeterminer slot (not all the students)
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (not all students) and uncountable nouns (not all information), plus a singular countable when another determiner or a time span follows (not all my life, not all day) — the same range as all, since it is all with a negative bolted on the front.
entries.ofRule: Optional before another determiner — not all (of) the students. Required before a pronoun — not all of them, ✗ not all them.
entries.pattern: Not all [plural/uncountable noun] + verb / not all (of) the [noun] / not all of [them/us/you] / Not all [noun] are [adjective]
entries.contrast: This entry fixes the most damaging ambiguity in the file. Not all is partial negation — some yes, some no. No and none of are total negation — zero. Not all the seats were taken means some were empty; None of the seats were taken means every seat was empty. Keep not in front of all, because moving it onto the verb creates the ambiguity back again: All the seats weren't taken is read both ways and should be rewritten. The singular counterpart is not every.
entries.meaning: Denies that the whole set is covered, without denying any particular member — "some, but not the whole." The verb agrees with the noun, exactly as with all: Not all the money is accounted for, Not all the checks have cleared.
examples: Not all heroes wear capes.
Not all of the applicants were interviewed.
Not all the money has been accounted for.
Not all insurance policies cover flood damage.
Not all of them agreed with the decision.
She works most weekends, though not all of them.

entries.position: any is the central determiner; not negates the verb or the clause, not the noun phrase
entries.register: neutral — the ordinary spoken alternative to no
entries.goesWith: plural countable nouns (not any survivors) and uncountable nouns (not any money); a singular countable only with the abstract nouns that take any at all (not any reason to worry, not any chance of that). ✗ not any apple.
entries.ofRule: Follows any — not any of the students, not any of them; of is required before a determined phrase or a pronoun.
entries.pattern: [subject] + didn't/doesn't/isn't/haven't … any [noun] / There isn't any [noun] / without any [noun] / not any of [the/my + noun]
entries.contrast: not any and no mean the same thing and differ in position and force, and two rules decide which one you can use. (1) In subject position only no works: ✓ No students came, ✗ Not any students came. (2) After the verb both work, and no is the more emphatic and more written of the two: We found no survivors against We didn't find any survivors. The one absolute prohibition is stacking them: ✗ I have no any money is impossible in every variety of English — a clause gets one negative marker, and no and any are competing candidates for the job.
entries.meaning: The analytic way to negate a quantity: put the negative on the verb and let any carry the noun. This is the default in spoken American English, where no before a noun after the verb sounds formal or emphatic. The archaic pattern I have not any money, with not directly before any and no auxiliary, is dead in American English — modern usage requires do-support: I don't have any money.
examples: We didn't find any survivors.
There's not any point in waiting around for him.
She hasn't given me any reason to worry.
There isn't any hot water in the building this morning.
He left without any explanation.
I don't want any of these leftovers.
They haven't had any complaints about the new system.

entries.position: not negates the central determiner every, and the phrase fills the determiner slot
entries.register: neutral
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — not every student, not every day. Never a plural (✗ not every students), never an uncountable (✗ not every water), inheriting every's restriction exactly.
entries.ofRule: Never with bare every — ✗ not every of them. The partitive is not every one of — not every one of them.
entries.pattern: Not every [singular countable noun] + singular verb / not every one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun] / It is not every [noun] that … (literary)
entries.contrast: not every is the singular partner of not all, and both are partial: Not every student passed and Not all the students passed both mean some did and some did not. Neither means No student passed, which is total. Word order carries the whole meaning — Not every student passed is unambiguous, while Every student didn't pass can be read either way and should be rewritten.
entries.meaning: Denies that the coverage is complete, member by member, while leaving individual members untouched. The noun and the verb stay singular: Not every window opens.
examples: Not every student needs a lab section.
Not every window in the house opens.
Not every day is going to go this smoothly.
Not every one of them agreed to sign.
Not every problem has a technical fix.
Not every restaurant on that block takes reservations.

entries.position: not negates the phrase headed by the numeral one
entries.register: emphatic — used to make a point, not to state a plain fact
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only — not one person, not one complaint. Never a plural (✗ not one people), never an uncountable (✗ not one water).
entries.ofRule: Yes, and it is common — not one of the students, not one of them. Of is required before a determined phrase or a pronoun.
entries.pattern: Not one [singular countable noun] + singular verb / not one of [the/my + plural noun or pronoun] / not one single [noun]
entries.contrast: Not one is the most emphatic of the zero-quantity phrases because it makes the hearer count. The scale runs not any (plain) → no (firmer) → not a (emphatic) → not one / not a single (most emphatic). Against none of, not one of insists on the counting: none of the students came reports, not one of the students came complains. The verb is singular even after of + plural: Not one of them was on time.
entries.meaning: Denies a set down to its final unit, with the numeral doing the emphatic work. It appears most often in subject position, where fronting it puts the zero at the very head of the sentence.
examples: Not one person raised a hand.
Not one of the applicants had the right certification.
Not one of them offered to help clean up.
In three years he has missed not one deadline.
Not one complaint has come in since the update.
She sent out forty resumes and got not one reply.

entries.respell: not-soh-MUCH-az-uh · the weak forms do most of the work here. The /t/ of not flaps or goes unreleased, so reduces to /sə/, as to /əz/, and the article to /ə/, so the phrase runs together as [nɑt sə ˈmʌtʃ əzə] — and after without, where it lives most of the time, [wɪˈðaʊt sə ˈmʌtʃ əzə]. The single stress is on much
entries.position: the negative —
entries.register: emphatic and faintly literary; entirely ordinary in speech after without, and used in writing when a point is being made rather than a fact reported
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, since the phrase contains a — not so much as a word, without so much as a goodbye. Never a plural (✗ not so much as a words) and never a bare uncountable (✗ not so much as a money); to reach an uncountable you must put a unit noun in front of it — not so much as a drop of rain, not so much as a scrap of evidence, not so much as a dime of the money.
entries.pattern: without so much as a [singular countable noun] · [negated verb] + so much as a [noun] · There wasn't so much as a [noun] · not so much as a [unit noun] of [uncountable] · [negative] + so much as + [verb] (the adverbial twin)
entries.contrast: This sits at the top of the zero-quantity scale running through this file — not any (plain) → no (firmer) → not a (emphatic) → not one and not a single (most emphatic) → not so much as a, which adds the further claim that even the smallest imaginable instance is missing. It is a negative-polarity item and cannot stand on its own: a bare positive ✗ He gave me so much as a dollar is ungrammatical, and the phrase needs not, without, never, hardly, or a question to license it. Note the adverbial twin, which takes a verb where this takes a noun and is just as common: He didn't so much as look at me. And keep it clear of the connective not so much … as (not stupid so much as careless), which is a comparison and negates nothing at all.
entries.meaning: With of: Not directly — ✗ not so much as a of them. The partitive is not so much as one of: not so much as one of them offered to help. Denies a set down below its smallest member — "not even this much." So much as is a minimizer: it names the least the speaker can picture and then denies that too, which is why the construction almost always carries a grievance. Its commonest home by far is after without, where it reports a slight: she left without so much as a goodbye. The verb stays singular, agreeing with a: Not so much as a light was on in the building. A learner will meet all five of these constantly in speech, in song lyrics, in fiction, and in older writing, and needs to recognize them and know where they belong. Two of them — ain't no and concord no — are the same phenomenon seen from two angles, and both are stigmatized in edited writing. The other three carry no stigma at all; they are costumes. Nary a and its positive twin ary a are Appalachian and rural Southern dialect used on purpose, and never a — the ancestor of both, by way of the contracted ne'er a — is Early Modern English surviving in a handful of frozen phrases. None of those three doubles its negative, which is precisely what separates them from the two that do.
examples: She walked out without so much as a goodbye.
Three months of drought, and not so much as a drop of rain.
He read the whole contract and didn't find so much as a typo.
They took the job and never sent so much as a thank-you note.
