There wasn't so much as a chair left in the apartment.
He didn't so much as look up when I came in. — the adverbial twin, with a verb instead of a noun
✗ He gave me so much as a dollar. — ungrammatical on its own; the phrase needs not, without, or never to license it.

entries.type: negative determiner inside a negative-concord frame
entries.position: no is the central determiner; ain't is the negated verb
entries.register: nonstandard in edited American English — systematic and rule-governed in African American English, in Southern and Appalachian vernacular, and in casual speech everywhere, but out of place in academic writing, business correspondence, and any formal register
entries.goesWith: whatever no goes with — singular countable (ain't no way), plural countable (ain't no jobs), and uncountable (ain't no money). The restriction on this phrase is social, not grammatical.
entries.ofRule: Not directly; the partitive is ain't none of, which doubles the concord again (There ain't none of them left).
entries.pattern: There ain't no [noun] / [subject] ain't got no [noun] / Ain't no [noun] + verb
entries.contrast: This is negative concord: the negative is marked twice, once on the verb (ain't) and once on the determiner (no). Standard American English marks it once and fills the second slot with any — There isn't any way, I don't have any money. The dialectal versions are neither confused nor illogical; they follow a consistent rule that many languages, including Spanish and French, use as their standard. What makes them nonstandard is social convention, not logic. Standard equivalents: ain't no way → isn't any way / is no way; ain't got no money → don't have any money / have no money.
entries.meaning: The most visible form of negative concord in American English, fixed enough in songs, titles, and catchphrases (Ain't No Sunshine, ain't no thing) that it functions almost as an idiom. Recognize it, understand the grammar behind it, and keep it out of your own writing unless you are quoting or writing dialogue.
examples: There ain't no way I'm driving in this weather. — nonstandard; standard: There isn't any way I'm driving in this weather.
He ain't got no patience for that kind of thing. — nonstandard; standard: He has no patience for that kind of thing.
Ain't no point in arguing about it now. — nonstandard; standard: There's no point in arguing about it now.
There ain't no jobs left in that town. — nonstandard; standard: There aren't any jobs left in that town.
She ain't got no time for excuses. — nonstandard; standard: She has no time for excuses.
Ain't no mountain high enough to keep me from you. — the song title, and a fair sample of the idiom in the wild

entries.respell: AIR-ee · with the article, ary a /ˈɛri ə/ · AIR-ee-uh · the vowel is the one in hair, matching nary a exactly; some speakers say /ˈæri/ (ARR-ee). The article keeps its weak /ə/, and in fast speech the whole phrase reduces to [ˈɛrə] or further to arn [ɑrn]. The word is a worn-down e'er a, "ever a" — the positive counterpart of ne'er a, "never a," which gave nary
entries.position: with the article,
entries.register: dialectal — Appalachian, Ozark, and rural Southern speech, and now largely a marker of older or rural speakers. An American meets it in Appalachian fiction and oral history, in old-time and bluegrass lyrics, and from relatives in the mountain South. It belongs to no written standard, and outside dialogue a writer using it will be read as imitating an accent
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, since the usual form contains a — ary a match, ary a soul, ary one. Never a plural (✗ ary a matches), never an uncountable (✗ ary a money). The bare form takes a singular countable too: ary man, ary bit.
entries.pattern: Have you got ary a [singular countable noun]? · [negated verb] + ary a [noun] · if ary [noun] · ary a one (of …) · ary [noun] (bare, the oldest form)
entries.contrast: ary is the positive member of a pair and nary a the negative one: ary a means "any," nary a means "not a single." Do you have ary a match? asks; I've got nary a match denies. Standard English fills the same two slots with any and not a, and the mapping is exact — ary a → any, nary a → not a. The two words have had very different careers: nary a escaped the mountains and became a national literary flourish that costs a writer nothing, while ary stayed home and is still heard as regional speech rather than as style. Note that it is not negative concord — ary a takes one negative per clause like any standard form, and in that it is unlike ain't no.
entries.meaning: With of: Not directly — ✗ ary a of them. The idiom is ary a one: ary a one of them. A dialectal free-choice determiner meaning "any, a single," descended from e'er a — "ever a." It survives almost entirely in questions, negatives, and conditionals, which is exactly the polarity profile of standard any, and it clusters around the same short list of nouns as nary a: one, soul, word, bit, match, dime. Learn to read it; do not write it outside dialogue or quotation.
examples: Have you got ary a match on you? — a question, where the word lives
I asked around, but there wasn't ary a soul who'd seen him. — a negative
If ary one of you knows better, speak up now. — a conditional, and the bare form
He never had ary a dime to his name. — dialect speech; standard: He never had a dime to his name.
"Did ary a letter come today?" she asked from the porch. — the phrase as a novelist sets it down
Not ary bit of that story is true. — the bare form, now the rarest of the three
Standard American English says any in every one of these sentences. — the whole mapping in one line

entries.position: nary negates the phrase headed by the central determiner a
entries.register: dialectal and literary — Appalachian and rural Southern in origin, now used nationally as a deliberately folksy or old-fashioned flourish; never neutral, but not stigmatized either
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, since the phrase contains a — nary a soul, nary a word. Never a plural (✗ nary a words), never an uncountable (✗ nary a money).
entries.ofRule: Not used — ✗ nary a of them. The idiom is nary a one: nary a one of them showed up.
entries.pattern: nary a [singular countable noun] / nary a one (of …) / There was nary a [noun] in sight
entries.contrast: It is a stylistic variant of not a and not one, filling the same grammatical slot but carrying a strong regional and archaic flavor. Where not a soul was there is plain English, nary a soul was there is a costume. Unlike the negative-concord forms in this section, nary a is not heard as an error — it is dialect deployed on purpose, and it takes only one negative per clause like any standard form.
entries.meaning: An old-fashioned emphatic negative meaning "not a single one." It survives in fiction, folk speech, and journalism reaching for color, and it almost always precedes a small set of nouns: soul, word, sound, drop, penny, one.
examples: There was nary a soul on the road at that hour.
He worked all winter and got nary a word of thanks.
Three months of drought and nary a drop of rain.
She asked all six of them and nary a one would answer.
The old barn stood there with nary a nail out of place.
We waited an hour, and nary a bus came by.

entries.respell: NEV-ur-uh · the article keeps its weak /ə/ throughout, and never itself has no weak form, since it carries the negation. In fast and older speech the medial /v/ drops and the two words run to [ˈnɛɚ ə] or [ˈnɛrə] — which is the exact road that produced the written contraction ne'er a /nɛr ə/ · NAIR-uh, and one step further, dialectal nary a /ˈnɛri ə/. The three spellings are one word at three stages of erosion
entries.register: archaic as a productive determiner; alive only inside fixed phrases. An American meets the old determiner use in Shakespeare and his contemporaries and in older poetry, and nowhere in modern prose. What survives in ordinary speech is the frozen never a dull moment and the deliberately old-fashioned idiom never a one
entries.goesWith: singular countable nouns only, since the phrase contains a — never a word, never a dull moment, never a one. Never a plural (✗ never a words), never an uncountable (✗ never a money). Do not mistake the live modern pattern for this one: in He never wrote a word, never is an ordinary adverb on the verb and a is just the article, and that pattern takes any noun the verb will allow.
entries.pattern: never a [singular countable noun] (the archaic determiner) · ne'er a [singular countable noun] (the same determiner in its contracted spelling, the form verse uses to save a syllable) · Never a dull moment (frozen) · never a one (of …) · never a whit (archaic) · [subject] + never + [verb] + a [noun] (the ordinary modern pattern, a different construction)
entries.contrast: The entry exists to separate two things that look identical on the page. (1) In Early Modern English never a was a genuine determiner meaning "not a single, no" — never a man in the company would speak meant "not one man." (2) In modern American English never is an adverb of frequency negating the verb, and a is simply the article: She never sent a thank-you note. The determiner is gone; the fossils are what is left of it. Against not a, which fills the same slot and is fully alive, never a adds "not even once, ever" — time rather than count. Against nary a, the relation is genealogical rather than stylistic: never a → ne'er a → nary a, one worn-down step at a time, and of the three only nary a is still productive, in dialect. Its positive counterpart, by the same derivation, is ary / ary a, from e'er a.
entries.meaning: With of: Not directly — ✗ never a of them. The idiom is never a one: never a one of them answered. An archaic emphatic negative meaning "not a single one." Its life as a productive determiner ended centuries ago, and it survives in two places: the stock phrase never a dull moment, which every American says and nobody parses, and the idiom never a one, which reads as costume. Written ne'er a, it is the form poets used to save a syllable, and it is the form from which dialectal nary a was worn down — so never a, ne'er a, and nary a are not three words but one word photographed at three ages. The verb is singular: Never a word was spoken.
examples: Never a dull moment around here. — the one fully live use, frozen solid
She asked all six of them and never a one would answer. — the surviving idiom, deliberately old-fashioned
Never a man in the company would speak against him. — the Early Modern determiner, meaning "not one man"; this is the use you meet in Shakespeare and nowhere in modern prose
He worked ten years there and got ne'er a word of thanks. — the contracted spelling, as verse and older prose set it down
In three months of drought there was never a drop of rain. — the phrase reached for as period flavor
She never sent a thank-you note. — the ordinary modern pattern: never is an adverb on the verb and a is just the article
Modern American writing says not a word of thanks, dialect says nary a word of thanks, and never a word of thanks is the antique. — the three registers in one line

entries.type: negative determiner inside a negative-concord frame
entries.position: central determiner, in a clause whose verb is already negated
entries.register: nonstandard in edited American English — fully systematic in African American English, Southern and Appalachian vernacular, Chicano English, and casual speech across the country, but read as an error in academic, professional, and published prose
entries.goesWith: the same three noun types as standard no — singular countable (I don't have no car), plural countable (He didn't make no promises), uncountable (We don't have no time). Nothing about the noun blocks it; the objection is entirely social.
entries.ofRule: The partitive doubles the concord too — I don't want none of that, where standard English has I don't want any of that.
entries.pattern: [subject] + don't/doesn't/didn't/won't + [verb] + no [noun] / There isn't/ain't no [noun] / [subject] + never + [verb] + no [noun]
entries.contrast: Standard American English marks negation once per clause and fills the second slot with any: I don't have any money, not I don't have no money. Keep two facts apart. (1) Don't … no is negative concord — nonstandard but perfectly grammatical inside its own dialects, and it does not cancel into a positive. (2) ✗ I have no any money is impossible in every variety, standard or vernacular, because no and any are two candidates for one job; no English speaker anywhere produces it. Note also that standard English does have a genuine cancelling double negative, carried by contrastive stress: I don't have NO money — I just don't have much means the speaker has some.
entries.meaning: Negative concord, popularly the "double negative": the single negative meaning of the clause is spelled out twice, once on the verb and once on the determiner. It does not reverse the meaning — I don't have no money means the speaker has none, exactly as I don't have any money does. English used concord as its standard through Chaucer's day, and Spanish, French, Russian, and Portuguese still do; it became stigmatized in English only after eighteenth-century grammarians applied an argument from arithmetic to it. Learn to hear it and understand it; do not write it outside dialogue or quotation.
examples: I don't have no money. — nonstandard; standard: I don't have any money.
He didn't make no promises. — nonstandard; standard: He didn't make any promises.
We ain't got no room for that. — nonstandard; standard: We don't have any room for that.
She never gave me no trouble. — nonstandard; standard: She never gave me any trouble.
There wasn't no reason to call. — nonstandard; standard: There wasn't any reason to call.
✗ I have no any money. — impossible in every variety of English; say I have no money or I don't have any money.
